planting.note: Divide offsets or root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; this Oaxacan species clusters readily at the base, so established clumps can be pulled apart and repotted with minimal disturbance.

directions: Grow in gritty, mineral succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering deeply and then allowing the soil to dry completely before watering again. Native to rocky slopes in Oaxaca, Mexico, this species forms tight clusters of short-stemmed rosettes with thick, blue-grey leaves that take on a dusty pink cast under strong light and cool temperatures. It offsets readily from the base to form spreading mounds, and loose sprays of small star-shaped flowers appear on wiry stalks in late winter to spring. Protect from prolonged wet soil and hard frost, bringing potted specimens under cover below the mid-20s F.

planting.note: Separate rooted suckers or root individual rosettes as cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; the species spreads by underground stolon-like suckers, so a single plant will fill a shallow pot with offsets over a season or two.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright, filtered light to a few hours of direct morning sun, letting the mix dry out fully between waterings. Discovered in Oaxaca, Mexico and named for succulent botanist and photographer Charles Glass, this species produces small, waxy, grey-white rosettes on short stems that spread outward from underground suckers to form loose colonies rather than a single clump. Leaf color stays pale silvery grey even in strong light, giving it a frosted look distinct from its more pink-blushed relatives. Small pale flowers appear on short stalks in spring; keep it in a shallow, wide container to accommodate its spreading habit.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, letting the cut ends callus for a few days before inserting; the sticky, glandular stems root readily and are best grown trailing from a hanging basket.

directions: Grow in gritty, mineral succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering thoroughly and then letting the mix dry out completely before the next watering. This Mexican species is named for the fine, sticky glandular hairs that coat its slender, trailing stems, which carry small, plump grey-green leaves in loose rosettes toward the tips. The tacky stem surface distinguishes it at a glance from smoother-stemmed relatives like Pachyphytum hookeri. Small bell-shaped flowers appear on short stalks in cooler months; grow it in a hanging basket or raised pot so the lax stems can cascade freely.

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; the thick coating of powdery farina rubs off easily with handling, so cuttings are best taken and set with minimal contact to preserve the chalky bloom.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, allowing the soil to dry out completely between waterings. This species carries some of the heaviest powdery farina in the genus, coating its plump, egg-shaped leaves in a pale blue-grey bloom that intensifies in strong light and cool weather. Rosettes stay compact and low, clumping slowly by basal offsets rather than trailing. Handle plants carefully and avoid overhead watering, since fingerprints and water spots permanently mar the delicate waxy coating.

common_name: Bashful Graptoveria (Dusty Rose Compact Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a named hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so propagation is strictly vegetative.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the mix dry out completely before rewatering. This compact Graptopetalum-Echeveria hybrid forms neat, tightly packed rosettes of pale blue-green leaves that blush a soft dusty pink to coral along the margins and tips when grown in strong light and cool conditions. Its small size and free-offsetting habit make it well suited to dish gardens and mixed succulent bowls. Bring containers indoors or under cover when temperatures drop toward freezing, since the fleshy leaves are easily damaged by frost.

common_name: Silver Star Graptoveria (Fuzzy White Starfish Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or individual leaves in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun; the finely fuzzy leaf surface holds excess moisture longer than smooth-leaved relatives, so let the mix dry thoroughly before each watering.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun, watering only once the mix has dried out completely. A cross involving the bristle-tipped Graptopetalum filiferum, this hybrid produces flattened, star-shaped rosettes of narrow, silvery-white leaves covered in a fine fuzz that gives the whole plant a frosted, velvety look. It stays low and slowly clumps by offsetting, making a striking textural contrast next to glossy or glaucous succulents. Keep leaves dry when watering to avoid rot at the fuzzy leaf bases.

common_name: Douglas Huth Graptoveria (Large Lavender-Blue Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light; this hybrid forms a substantial solitary rosette, so allow generous room in the container before it needs repotting.

directions: Grow in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings. This large-growing hybrid forms broad, symmetrical rosettes of thick, powdery lavender-blue leaves that deepen toward purple with strong sun and temperature stress, echoing the coloring of Echeveria 'Perle von Nurnberg' but on a bigger scale. It stays mostly solitary rather than clumping, so mature specimens make a dramatic single focal rosette in a container or bed. Provide excellent drainage and protect from frost, moving potted plants under cover when temperatures approach freezing.

common_name: Blue Giant Sedeveria (Chunky Pale Blue-Green Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets, stem sections, or individual leaves in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun; this cultivar grows larger and more robust than most Sedeveria, so give it extra room to reach full size.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun, watering deeply and then letting the mix dry out completely before watering again. True to its name, this Sedum-Echeveria hybrid produces unusually large, chunky rosettes of thick, pale blue-green leaves that can take on a warm apricot blush at the tips under bright light and cooler temperatures. It offsets from the base over time to form a small cluster of substantial rosettes rather than a single trailing stem. Sprays of small star-shaped flowers appear on branched stalks in late spring; protect from hard frost and prolonged wet soil.

common_name: Green Rose Sedeveria (Ruffled Jade-Green Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light; the tightly overlapping leaves shed water readily, so avoid letting moisture pool in the rosette center after watering.

directions: Grow in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the mix dry out completely between waterings. This hybrid forms a tight, low rosette of overlapping, incurved jade-green leaves that ruffle and cup inward much like the petals of an unopened rose, an effect that becomes more pronounced under bright light. Color stays a rich uniform green rather than blushing with stress, making it a good textural contrast to pink- or blue-toned succulents nearby. It clumps slowly by basal offsets and suits small containers, dish gardens, or the front edge of a succulent bed.

common_name: Darley Dale Sedeveria (Powdery Blue-Grey Branching Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light; older plants naturally branch and sprawl, so stake, prune, or restart leggy stems from cuttings to keep a tidy shape.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun, watering thoroughly and then allowing the mix to dry out completely before the next watering. One of the older named Sedum-Echeveria hybrids in cultivation, this cultivar forms powdery blue-grey rosettes on stems that branch and lengthen with age, eventually sprawling into a loose, shrubby clump rather than staying compact. The farina-coated leaves resist water spotting better than many glossier succulents, making it a durable choice for outdoor beds in mild climates. Pinch or take cuttings from leggy growth periodically to encourage fuller, more compact rosettes.

common_name: Francesco Baldi Graptosedum (Blue-Grey to Pink Trailing Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, letting cut ends callus for several days first; stems lengthen and trail with age, so this hybrid is best grown in a hanging basket or spilling over a wall.

directions: Grow in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting the mix dry out completely between waterings. A widely grown cross of Graptopetalum paraguayense and Sedum pachyphyllum, this hybrid produces plump, blue-grey leaves in loose rosettes along trailing stems, shifting to warm rosy pink and lavender tones under bright light and cool weather. Its vigorous, cascading growth makes it a popular choice for hanging containers, retaining walls, and mixed succulent troughs. Snap off and replant fallen leaf rosettes to quickly propagate additional plants.

common_name: Vera Higgins Graptosedum (Bronze-Orange Trailing Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or fallen leaves in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix; older stems trail and lengthen, so periodic pruning and restarting cuttings keeps the planting dense rather than sparse and leggy.

directions: Plant in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun, watering deeply and then letting the mix dry out completely before watering again. This classic hybrid between Graptopetalum and Sedum forms loose rosettes of thick, spoon-shaped leaves that flush a distinctive bronze to burnt-orange color when grown hard in full sun with sparse water, fading to green-grey in shadier or richer conditions. It is a parent of several brighter-colored sports sold under other cultivar names, but keeps a more muted, earthy tone of its own. Grow it in a hanging basket, rock garden, or trailing over a container edge for the best display of its trailing habit.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or individual fallen leaves in spring in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun; the strongest coral-pink color develops under bright light and lean, dry conditions rather than shade or rich soil.

directions: Grow in gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in full sun, letting the soil dry out completely between waterings for the brightest color. Arising as a more vividly colored sport of Graptosedum 'Vera Higgins', this cultivar produces trailing stems of plump, spoon-shaped leaves that turn a glowing coral-pink to peachy orange when stressed by strong sun and cool temperatures, echoing the alpenglow light for which it is named. Growth is vigorous and trailing, quickly filling a hanging basket or spilling over the edge of a raised bed. Snap off leaves or stem tips and let them callus before rooting to propagate new plants easily.

common_name: Scheidecker's Pachyveria (Classic Blue-Grey Chunky Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light; as a named hybrid cultivar it does not come true from seed, so propagation is strictly vegetative.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering thoroughly and then letting the mix dry out completely before the next watering. One of the oldest recorded succulent hybrids, dating to the 1870s and combining Pachyphytum bracteosum with an Echeveria parent, this cultivar forms chunky, symmetrical rosettes of thick, blue-grey leaves with a soft powdery coating. It clumps modestly by basal offsets rather than trailing, keeping a tidy, compact profile in containers. Handle the leaves carefully, since the powdery bloom marks easily and does not regenerate once rubbed off.
